notes: "Athena showed you all this." / "No one showed me." - 'taught' is the natural verb and is beginner vocabulary: "Athena taught you all this." / "No one taught me." This also avoids a clash with the later 'Athena showed the gods on her loom'.
"Arachne's hair fell away." - 'fell out' is the everyday phrasal verb for hair; consider "Arachne's hair fell out."
"Athena heard about these words." - slightly stiff; "Athena heard these words." or "Athena heard about this."
Words a beginner may not know (goddess, among, change her mind, learn a lesson) are few and are either explained in the text ('Athena was a goddess') or clear from context, so comprehension holds.
"They both worked quickly, and their threads moved like light." - the simile is a little odd; "their threads flew back and forth" is more natural.

"At the sides, she made four small pictures of people." - the original places these scenes in the four corners, as B1-C1 do; "In the four corners, she made four small pictures of people." would keep levels consistent.
"People wanted to touch the pictures because they looked so real." is an invented but harmless detail.
"This made the goddess even angrier." - Athena has not been described as angry before in this level; "This made the goddess very angry." reads more cleanly.
'disguise' and 'sprinkled' are slightly above B1 but fully clear from context.
"whose family was far from important" and "Her little town was of no importance" repeat the same idea in one paragraph; one could be trimmed.

"The king of the gods sat in the middle" followed by "In the center she showed her own contest" places two things in the center; "Before them she showed her own contest..." would avoid the slight spatial confusion (the same applies to C1).

"she placed a smaller scene, meant as a warning to her rival, of mortals who had dared..." - the inserted phrase separates 'scene' from 'of mortals'; "she placed a smaller scene of mortals who had dared to compete with the gods, meant as a warning to her rival" flows better.

summary: A faithful retelling of Ovid's Arachne (Metamorphoses VI): humble dyer's daughter, nymph visitors, Athena's disguise and warning, the reveal and blush, the two tapestries (twelve gods, contest with the sea god, four warning corners, olive border vs. the gods' deceptions with a flower border), the faultless work torn apart, and the herb-juice transformation. Arachne's hanging and the shuttle blows are omitted and the gods' misdeeds are softened, which is appropriate for a 4+ rating; grammar fits each level and all quizzes have single, correct keyed answers. Only minor wording notes remain.
